R2.2.response: We accept the correction and have gone further than softening the wording. The earlier claim rested on removing three features chosen by inspection, which as the reviewer says establishes very little. The revision defines the suspect set objectively, as every feature whose single-feature AUC reaches 0.99, and removes the whole of it. Five features meet that bar, all of them entropy features. Macro F1 with them removed is 97.94% with a bootstrap interval of [97.86, 98.02], against 97.88% [97.81, 97.97] for the full model. The intervals overlap, so the removal changes nothing measurable. We also report what that does and does not license: it rules out a narrow leakage explanation concentrated in a few columns, and it simultaneously shows the discriminative information is distributed widely enough that feature ablation alone cannot establish the model has learned attack behavior. Both halves are now in the text, and the limitations section states plainly that dataset-specific artifacts cannot be excluded by any experiment we can run on a single synthetic corpus.
R2.2.action: Replaced the three-feature ablation with a progressive removal study over an objectively defined suspect set, added bootstrap confidence intervals, and rewrote the surrounding claims. The word "confirms" no longer appears in this context.

R3.1.response: Yes, and this is now the centerpiece of the leakage analysis. Defining "known leaking features" by intuition would have reproduced the weakness of the earlier ablation, so we define the suspect set by measurement: any feature that separates the classes on its own at AUC 0.99 or above. Five features qualify. With all five removed the detector reaches 97.94% macro F1 against 97.88% for the full feature set, and removing the ten most separable features raises it to 98.69%. Detection does not depend on the columns most likely to be generator artifacts. Three further checks support the same conclusion: no feature has class-disjoint ranges, no test flow has a feature-identical twin in the training partition after deduplication, and the median standardized distance from a test flow to its nearest training neighbor is 0.142 with none closer than 1e-6. A label-permutation control collapses the pipeline to chance (macro F1 0.4978, AUC 0.5027), which is the prerequisite for trusting any of the above.
R3.1.action: Added a full leakage audit with an objective suspect definition, progressive removal through the entire flagged set, distribution checks, nearest-neighbor analysis, and two controls.
R3.1.location: Sec. VII-D and Table 8; the single-feature separability probe is reported in Sec. VII-C

R3.2.response: Thank you for raising this; it is a fair criticism and we should have done it in the first place. No collinearity diagnostics were applied in the earlier version, which was an omission. They have now been run and the answer is not flattering to the feature set. Of 3,828 feature pairs, 61 exceed |r| = 0.95 and 19 exceed 0.99. Of the 76 non-constant features, 55 have a variance inflation factor above 10 and 32 above 100, the median VIF is 51.4, and the design matrix condition number is 3.9e16. We then measured whether the attributions survive that redundancy. Across ten seeds the five highest-attributed features are identical in every run, with the full attribution vectors correlating at Spearman 0.956 and never below 0.932. Beyond rank five the ranking is not reproducible: top-10 Jaccard averages 0.710 and falls to 0.538, and across bootstrap resamples top-5 Jaccard drops to 0.767. The operational conclusion is stated explicitly in the text: an operator reading the top five contributing features is looking at a stable explanation, while inferring anything from the difference between the eighth and twelfth ranked feature is reading noise. On reduction, correlation clustering from 88 to 50 features raises macro F1 to 97.99% and halves per-flow inference cost, so the reduced set is strictly better on both axes.
R3.2.action: Added correlation, VIF and conditioning diagnostics, a feature-reduction study, and a SHAP stability analysis across ten seeds and ten bootstrap resamples.
R3.2.location: Sec. VII-G (Collinearity, redundancy, and attribution stability), Table 11

R6.4.response: The objection is well posed and we measured it rather than arguing. Two things had to be corrected first. The equation printed in the submitted manuscript was not the recurrence the implementation executes, and the printed form is only valid while the window length is constant, so it is wrong during warm-up. The revision prints the running-sum recurrence the code actually runs. On drift, a stream of 12,000,000 admit and evict updates over 65,524 distinct keys was compared against exact recomputation at 240 checkpoints, with a rational-arithmetic evaluation confirming the float64 reference is itself exact. Maximum accumulated drift is 7.5e-14 bits for the implemented form and 2.3e-13 bits for the equation as previously printed. Converting that to the quantity that matters, perturbing all eight entropy features of all 1,077,238 test flows by the worst-case magnitude changes zero decisions. Compensated summation and periodic resynchronization were also measured and buy no accuracy at this scale, so neither is enabled. Incidentally, the printed phi-form is both three times less accurate and nearly twice as slow as the implemented one.
R6.4.action: Corrected the equation to match the implementation, added a numerical-stability study with three mitigations, and reported the decision-level impact.
R6.4.location: Eqs. (9)-(11) in Sec. V-B, Sec. V-C, and Sec. VII-I

R6.6.response: The reviewer is right and the measurements are worse than the comment implies. Fifty-five of the 76 non-constant features have VIF above 10 and 32 above 100, with a condition number of 3.9e16. Separately, twelve of the 80 exported flow statistics are constant across all 3,590,794 flows of this partition and carry no information at all. We note in particular that FIN_Flag_Count is one of them, and that the submitted manuscript ranked it among the three most influential features, which cannot be true of a column that never varies. The recomputed attributions do not rank it. On the practical question, reducing the feature set by correlation clustering from 88 to 50 features raises macro F1 from 97.88% to 97.99% and halves per-flow inference latency, so the redundancy was costing both accuracy and speed.
R6.6.action: Added collinearity diagnostics, identified the constant features, corrected the attribution ranking, and added a feature-reduction study showing the reduced set dominates the full one.
R6.6.location: Sec. VII-C (Feature-set audit), Sec. VII-G (Collinearity, redundancy, and attribution stability), Table 11

R6.7.response: Agreed, and acting on it revealed a deeper problem with the corpus. All threshold analysis now uses the precision-recall plane, with average precision reported alongside ROC-AUC and the chance baseline stated explicitly, because at 97.2% positive prevalence a classifier drawing at random scores AP 0.97 while ROC-AUC stays at 0.5. Threshold selection is performed on a validation block carved chronologically from the training partition, never on test data. What that exposed is that the validation block contains only 60 benign flows, because benign traffic in this capture is concentrated almost entirely at the end of the recording. Sixty negatives cannot support a stable threshold estimate, and we say so rather than presenting the selected value as tuned. The selected threshold is reported, the test operating point is reported once, and the underlying limitation is documented.
R6.7.action: Replaced the FNR-based sweep with precision-recall analysis, moved selection to a validation block, and documented why the corpus cannot support reliable threshold tuning.
R6.7.location: Sec. IV-C, Sec. VII-H (Threshold selection on the precision-recall plane), Sec. VI-B

R6.8.response: The reviewer's alternative explanation is the correct one, and we tested it directly rather than defending the original claim. Removing the top three features changes macro F1 from 97.88% to 97.89%. Removing the top five, which is the entire objectively flagged suspect set, gives 97.94%. Removing the top ten gives 98.69%, better than the full feature set. The redundancy is exactly as deep as the reviewer suspected, and the collinearity diagnostics quantify why: 55 of 76 non-constant features have VIF above 10. We now state the negative conclusion in the text: feature-removal ablation on this corpus cannot establish that the model has learned attack behavior, because the information is distributed too widely for any small removal to be informative. R7.8.response: This comment led to the most consequential correction in the revision, and we would rather state it plainly than bury it. The submitted manuscript described a temporal split in which all training flows precede all test flows. The reported figures were produced by a stratified random split. We established this three ways: the reported test class counts of 9,311 and 1,068,487 are exactly 30% of each class, which a stratified split produces by construction; re-running the stratified split reproduces the published macro F1 to within 0.016 points; and the released code calls train_test_split with stratification after sorting by timestamp, so the sort is performed and the ordering then discarded. Under a genuine chronological split, macro F1 is 97.85% rather than 99.96%. The revision adopts the chronological protocol as primary, reports the stratified result beside it, and quantifies the gap. Documentation has been added throughout: split definitions, a validation block used for all tuning, nested cross-validation with forward-chaining outer folds, and an explicit statement that the test partition is read once. We also report that hyperparameter selection is unstable on this corpus, choosing five different configurations across five outer folds.
R7.8.action: Corrected the protocol, reported both splits, added a protocol subsection, ran nested cross-validation with forward-chaining folds, and documented the tuning and test separation.
R7.8.location: Sec. VI-B (Evaluation protocol), which now defines both validation blocks, the subsampled protocol and the nested-CV grid; Sec. VII-A (Sensitivity to the evaluation protocol) and Table 6; Sec. VII-B
